message.content:
**Ionisation – choosing “the best” depends entirely on your goal** Below is a quick‑reference guide that matches typical applications to the most suitable ionisation technique(s), along with key advantages / disadvantages so you can decide which one fits *your* needs best. | Application | Preferred Technique(s) | Why it’s often chosen | |-------------|------------------------|-----------------------| | **Mass Spectrometry (proteomics, metabolomics)** | • Electrospray Ionisation (ESI)
• Matrix‐Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionisation (MALDI) | - **ESI:** soft, produces multiply charged ions → high m/z range; ideal for peptides/proteins.
- **MALDI:** fast sample prep, tolerant of salts & contaminants; great for large biomolecules and imaging MS. | | **Small organic molecules (<500 Da)** | • Atmospheric Pressure Chemical Ionisation (APCI)
• Electron Impact (EI) (in GC–MS) | - **APCI:** gentle yet efficient for moderately polar compounds; works well at atmospheric pressure.
- **EI:** hard ionisation gives reproducible fragmentation patterns essential for library matching. | | **Nonpolar organics, gases** | • Direct Inlet Gas Chromatography (GC) EI
• Photoionisation (PI) | - **EI** provides characteristic fragment spectra.
- **PI** offers softer ionisation, useful when preserving molecular ions is critical. | | **Trace gas detection (environmental monitoring)** | • Proton Transfer Reaction (PTR)
• Selected Ion Flow Tube (SIFT) | Both give real‑time, highly sensitive measurements without chromatographic separation. | | **Surface analysis / thin films** | • Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry (SIMS) | Provides depth profiling and elemental mapping down to sub‑nm resolution. | | **High‑throughput screening (e.g., drug discovery)** | • Rapid Evaporative Ionisation Mass Spectrometry (REIMS)/DESI | Enables direct sampling from biological tissues or liquids with minimal preparation. | --- ### Quick Decision Tree 1. **What size/mass range do you target?** - >1000 Da → **MALDI** (or nano‑electrospray) - 200–1500 Da → **ESI** (for proteins/peptides) or **APCI** (small metabolites) 2. **Do you need structural fragments for identification?** - Yes → Use **EI** (if compatible with GC) or **CID/MS²** after initial ionisation (ESI/APCI). 3. **Is speed/sample throughput crucial?** - High throughput → **Rapid evaporative/DESI**, **LC‑MS** workflows. 4. **Are samples nonvolatile or thermally labile?** - Nonvolatile → **Soft ionisers** such as ESI/MALDI; avoid EI unless coupled to LC. 5. **Need surface or spatially resolved data?** - Imaging → **MALDI-MSI** or **DESI-MSI**. --- #### A Few Practical Tips | Tip | Explanation | |-----|--------------| | **Use a dual‑mode source** (ESI/APCI) | Many modern instruments allow switching between modes mid‑run, giving flexibility across analytes. | | **Optimize solvent composition** | For ESI, aqueous-organic mixtures with ~0.1% formic acid work universally; adjust pH for better protonation/deprotonation. | | **Check matrix compatibility** | With MALDI, choose matrices that absorb near the laser wavelength (e.g., DHB, sinapinic acid); mismatched matrices lead to poor signal. | | **Beware of adducts** | Especially in ESI/APCI, sodium/potassium adducts may dominate; adding ammonium acetate helps suppress them. | | **Consider tandem MS** | Even the “softest” ioniser still benefits from MSⁿ experiments for definitive structure confirmation. | --- ### Bottom Line There isn’t a single “best” ionisation method—each has its niche: - **For complex proteomes** → **ESI** (often coupled to HPLC). - **For intact macromolecule imaging** → **MALDI**. - **For small volatile organics** → **EI** (GC–MS) or **APCI** (LC–MS). - **For trace environmental gases** → **PTR/SIFT**. Pick the technique whose strengths align with your analyte properties, required sensitivity, and workflow constraints. If you’re unsure, many labs run parallel tests on a few representative standards to benchmark performance before committing to a full protocol.
